subtopic: REPORT OF ACTIVITIES TO MARCH 31, 1943-SUBSIDIES PAID BY COMMODITY PRICES STABILIZATION CORPORATION TO MARCH 31, 1942.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REPORT OF ACTIVITIES TO MARCH 31, 1943-SUBSIDIES PAID BY COMMODITY PRICES STABILIZATION CORPORATION TO MARCH 31, 1942.
speechtext:
I desire to table two documents concerning the wartime prices and trade board. The first is a report covering the activities of the board from its creation on September 3, 1939, to March 31, 1943, a period of three years and seven months. This is the first detailed report of this kind prepared by the board and will, I feel sure, be of considerable interest to hon. members and to the public at large. An attempt has been

made to deal briefly yet adequately with all phases of the work of the board and its related crown companies, and I am hopeful that it will give information that would otherwise be requested on the order paper or when the relevant item in the war appropriation is under consideration, and thus will help to facilitate proceedings. Copies of the report are being distributed to hon. members to-day.
The second document I am tabling is a statement showing the recipients of subsidies paid by the commodity prices stabilization corporation up to March 31, 1942. The corporation was formed in December, 1941, and is the agency responsible, under the wartime prices and trade board, for the payment of subsidies necessary for the maintenance of the price ceiling. This statement covers subsidies paid during a period of approximately three months, January, February and March, 1942.
Hon. members may recall that a year ago- on April 23 to be precise-I gave a statement to the house in which I dealt at some length with the reasons for subsidies and the basis on which they are paid. At that time I said that I had come to the conclusion, after very careful study, that it is definitely not in the public interest to give current information as to the names of persons to whom subsidies are being paid, or the amount paid to each. I did agree, however, at some appropriate time, that is when the information is not likely to reveal to competitors and others intimate details of the nature and volume of the recipients' business, to give the names of individual recipients and the amount of subsidy paid to each. It is reasonable to assume, I think, that information as to subsidies paid more than a year ago is not likely to reveal anything of vital importance in regard to current business dealings.
The statement I am now tabling shows subsidy payments amounting to SI,180,215. As I have already explained, this covers only the initial four months of the price ceiling and represents but a small fraction of total subsidies paid to date. As hon. members will see, when they have had an opportunity of reading the full report of the wartime prices and trade board, total subsidies paid from the date of the application of the price ceiling until March 31, 1943, amounted to approximately S65 million, in addition to which there were trading losses on bulk purchases by the commodity prices stabilization corporation of about $2j4 million.
Although subsidies to the end of March, 1942, amounted to just over one million one hundred thousand dollars, no less than 35,601 individuals participated in the payments. This large number is attributable to the fact that

Wartime Prices and Trade Board
the most important subsidies during this period were domestic subsidies paid in connection with the production of fluid and concentrated milk. At that time a subsidy of 40 cents per 100 pounds was paid on milk used in the manufacture of concentrated milk products and 30 cents per 100 pounds on fluid milk sold in areas where there had been no price increase since August 1, 1941. These milk subsidies accounted for nearly 80 per cent of total subsidies paid to March 31, 1942, and for all but 129 of the individual recipients.
I am sure hon. members will appreciate the very heavy task involved in listing the names of 35,000 individual recipients of milk subsidies and will agree with me that the expenditure of time and money entailed in preparing such a list could not have been justified. Instead of giving the names of individual ultimate recipients of these milk subsidies, it was therefore decided to list the names of the milk distributors which had been used as agencies for making payments to individual milk producers, together with the numbers of producers participating. Thus one of the first names on the list is that of a Toronto dairy which was paid $15,053.00 to reimburse it for subsidies in that amount which it, as a milk distributor, had previously paid out in full to 404 producers delivering their milk to it.
Apart from milk the only other classifications of subsidies up to the end of March 1942 were footwear and imports. I would refer hon. members to the report of the board for details as to the principles on which these subsidies were paid. During the period covered by this statement $191,504 were paid out by way of domestic subsidy on leather footwear to 78 individual recipients and $64,758 on imports to 51 individual recipients. The statement does not specify the import or imports in respect of which subsidy was paid, listing only the name of the recipients and the total amount paid. To have classified payments by individual imported goods would have meant much additional work in the preparation of the statement and in particular cases might have meant, even after the lapse of more than twelve months, the revelation of information valuable to Competitors.
At the risk of reiterating in part what I said a year ago I want to make it perfectly clear that these subsidies are not really subsidies to any manufacturer, importer or dealer, but are in reality subsidies for the benefit of the consumer. They are paid when there is no other way of ensuring adequate supplies of a particular product for the consumer at prices
permitted by the price ceiling. In principle, these subsidies are paid to the consumer to keep down the cost of living. In practice, because consumers are so numerous, they are paid to producers or dealers on condition that they maintain supplies and carry out the policy of the price ceiling by supplying goods to others at such prices as will permit them in turn to operate within the limits of the price ceiling.
I can perhaps illustrate this point by referring to subsidies on imports. These are paid to ensure a continued supply of essential goods produced outside of Canada at costs higher than would permit their sale in Canada at domestic ceiling prices. If the subsidy were not paid, these essential goods simply would not be imported for sale in Canada at ceiling prices.
With regard to presenting a report later, covering subsidies paid in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1943, the difficulties in giving names of recipients, the chief of which is the tremendous number of individual payments-hundreds of thousands-will be sh great that it now appears that they will be insurmountable. I can discuss these difficulties when the wartime prices and trade board estimates under the War Appropriation Act are reached. My only purpose in referring to them now is that I do not wish it to be assumed that the procedure followed with regard to the subsidies paid in 1941-42 will or can necessarilj' be followed for those paid in 1942-43.

maintopic: INCREASE OF QUOTA FOR 1942-43 TO FIFTEEN BUSHELS PER AUTHORIZED ACRE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: INCREASE OF QUOTA FOR 1942-43 TO FIFTEEN BUSHELS PER AUTHORIZED ACRE
speechtext:
Before the orders of the
day are proceeded with I should like to make a brief statement respecting wheat quotas for this crop year.
The Canadian Wheat Board are establishing 1942-43 wheat quotas of fifteen bushels per authorized acre as quickly as elevator space permits. About eight hundred points can be increased to fifteen bushels almost immediately. Up to the present the maximum quotas have been fourteen bushels per authorized acre. The extra bushel is considered necessary to bring the permitted deliveries up to 280 million bushels, as provided in order in council No. 10,000 of November 6, 1942.
The authorized acreage for wheat delivery purposes in the west in 1942-43 is slightly over 19 million acres, but many farmers are unable to deliver fifteen bushels per authorized acre because of hail, drought, frost, et cetera, unusually heavy farm feeding of wheat, or because of seeding in 1942 much less than the authorized acreage for delivery purposes. The deliveries of durum wheat, military services over-deliveries, and certain family gristing deliveries are over and above the total delivery figure of 280 million bushels.
The authorized wheat acreage for delivery purposes in 1943-44 will be closer to 20 million acres than to 19 million acres, mainly because there are about 700.000 authorized acres on farms which seeded no wheat in 1942-43. This acreage was ineffective for delivery purposes in 1942-43, but some of it will be effective in 1943-44. The western farmers will begin the 1943-44 season with

200,000,000 to 225,000,000 bushels of wheat on farms, whereas they had practically none to start the 1942-43 season. With an ordinary 1943 crop, the authorized wheat acreage will therefore be more effective in 1943-44 than in 1942-43 and a fourteen bushel quota should bring out as much wheat in 1943-44 as a fifteen bushel quota will in 1942-43.

maintopic: INCREASE OF QUOTA FOR 1942-43 TO FIFTEEN BUSHELS PER AUTHORIZED ACRE
speechtext: Are we to understand from this statement that there will be space available at delivery points for the quotas that have been established at those points?

maintopic: INCREASE OF QUOTA FOR 1942-43 TO FIFTEEN BUSHELS PER AUTHORIZED ACRE
speechtext: The quotas will be established on a basis of fifteen bushels just as soon as there is space available at the various points, and it is hoped that the total amount of wheat which we have stated we would take from the producers will be accepted before the end of the crop season.

maintopic: INCREASE OF QUOTA FOR 1942-43 TO FIFTEEN BUSHELS PER AUTHORIZED ACRE
speechtext: How many points are there at which this quota cannot be accepted now?

maintopic: INCREASE OF QUOTA FOR 1942-43 TO FIFTEEN BUSHELS PER AUTHORIZED ACRE
speechtext: I forget the exact number of quota points, but there are eight hundred where this quota can be accepted, and I think that is about fifty per cent of the quota delivery points.

speechtext:
Yesterday I asked the Minister of Labour if he
would make a statement with reference to the availability of internees and prisoners of war. Is he ready to make the statement?
Hon, HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister of Labour): I have not forgotten the question addressed to me. Council, however, did not finish its deliberations to-day until almost three o'clock. I shall try to get the information for the hon. member on Monday.

I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Labour in reference to the matter of the allocation of man-power for farm labour, of which there is a definite shortage at the present time. What is being done, and what success has been attained in securing the services of conscientious objectors and others subject to alternative service to go to the farms at this time to assist in the spring work? I would ask, too. whether any measure of compulsion to that end is being applied.

The reply to the first question is this: There are 700,000 farms in Canada. Out of that 700,000 farms the number of applications for farm help stands at about 4,600. That is the figure this morning. I am not suggesting that that is a complete indication of the farm labour situation at present, but it will indicate to hon. members that at least, while the situation might be grave, it is not quite as grave as some people would have us believe.
They are not applying, that is all.

The machinery is there. With respect to conscientious objectors, the hon. member is no doubt aware that an order in council was passed about two weeks ago. We are now in process of setting up the machinery. A director has been appointed, and alternative selective service officers have been appointed to deal with the problem of conscientious objectors. It is not a big problem, compared with some problems with which we have to deal in a time of war. Speaking from memory I would say there are in Canada about 3,000 conscientious objectors of military age. Of that number I believe about 1,500-and again I speak from memory-are already in alternative services.
Doing what?

Some are in the forestry camps of British Columbia, some are doing
Sugar

fire prevention work, others are building roads in Alberta. They are engaged in undertakings of that kind. I believe it is fair to say that the great majority of conscientious objectors in Canada are at present engaged in agriculture, which in itself is a partial answer to the hon. member's question. He can rest assured that those who are available will be placed in a manner which will be in the best interests of the country, and where we can best use them.
Does that include those in the House of Commons?
Yes; if there are any, it includes them.
On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I should like to ask the Minister of Finance to make a statement, if he will, by way of explanation and clarification with regard to the policy followed by the wartime prices and trade board in the rationing of sugar to the housewives of Canada for canning purposes. My object in rising to seek such a statement from the minister is based upon this situation. Earlier this year the ration administration issued to the housewives of Canada an appeal which read in part as follows:
Home canning takes on new importance in wartime. We want as much as possible of Canada's perishable fruits, including wild fruits, canned for use throughout the winter.
It rests with Canadian homemakers to make the fullest use of Canada's fruit crop for wartime food. Any sugar allowed is in trust so that you may provide canned fruit, jam and jelly for your families during the winter months.
Later the housewives were asked to make formal application for the amount of sugar required for this purpose, and now some five hundred local volunteer ration boards throughout Canada have been asked to take the responsibility of restricting the amount of such sugar to a figure which is said to be well below one-half the amount actually applied for by the housewives of the dominion. The fact that the widespread appeal was made without indicating the limitations which were later instituted may very well have the effect of placing ah unnecessary burden upon the local ration boards throughout Canada and may well lead to the feeling in the minds of Canadian housewives that they have been encouraged to lay plans for fruit canning without having had the true picture given to them at the beginning. Protests appearing in the press would 
indicate that there is urgent need for the minister to make a full explanation and to clarify the matter at once.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, after I received notice of this question from my hon. friend I made inquiries about this matter. I find that the reason for what my hon. friend has called an appeal was that the ration administration was afraid applications would not be made in time for the sugar required for canning, and they brought the matter somewhat forcibly to the attention of the public in the language that has been quoted by the hon. gentleman. Their expectation was that they would receive applications for sugar sufficient to can the usual amount of fruit, and they were desirous of making available enough sugar for that purpose. As a matter of fact, however, they have received applications for 209,000,000 pounds, which is far more than enough to can the largest quantity of fruit that has ever been canned in Canada. The amount of fruit represented by that amount of sugar never was canned in this country and probably cannot be canned. One hundred million pounds of sugar, which is as much as has been used in the past, if not more, has been set aside for canning purposes. That being so, it is necessary to have the quantities requested in these applications reduced in the best why possible. It may be possible to increase somewhat the amount of sugar that will be available, but I cannot give any guarantee as to that.

In the advertisement
there was no suggestion of any limitation, and as I understand it from those who give me information on this point from time to time many housewives throughout the dominion regarded the appeal as something in the national interest; they regarded the preserving and canning of fruit as necessary in order that the man-power employed in the canning industry, in the manufacture of containers and so on, might be made available for other purposes. On top of that, the final burden rests upon the local ration board. I think the minister had better make it a little clearer to housewives so that they will not feel that a hoax of some description has been worked upon them. I know the minister has that in mind. But on the other hand one cannot ask the housewives of Canada to preserve and can all possible fruit, in the national interest, and then finally leave it to the local ration board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no justification for the suggestion of a hoax. Certainly the public would not understand that an unlimited

Mutual Aid Bill
amount of sugar was available, nor would the statement in the appeal make any difference in the amount of individual applications.
Why does the minister say that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ju^t because it stands to reason that if 100,000,000 pounds is available, how can one individual plan her application in regard to that 100,000,000 pounds. However, I shall not argue that. All I am saying is that the purpose of the appeal was to draw the attention of the public to the fact that applications for sugar for canning purposes should be made, and canning so encouraged.
It went much farther than that, of course.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: VICTORY OP ALLIED FORCES IN NORTH AFRICA- DAY OP PRAYER AND THANKSGIVING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, hon. members will have observed that yesterday the government of the United Kingdom set aside next Sunday, May 16, as a day of prayer and thanksgiving for the victory in North Africa. My colleagues and I feel that the people of Canada would, on the same day, wish to join in a like public expression of thanksgiving upon the victorious culmination of the African campaign. On behalf of the government I should therefore express the hope that throughout Canada religious services on Sunday next may be given a character appropriate to the occasion.

PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OP §1,000,000,000 FOR PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER OP WAR SUPPLIES
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY moved the third reading of Bill No. 76, for granting to His Majesty aid for the purpose of making available Canadian war supplies to the united nations.

Mr. Speaker, this is a bill to transfer to the united nations goods to the value of one billion dollars as a contribution to the common cause. As 'such we support the third reading of the bill. During the discussion in committee we refrained largely from making any criticism of its principles because we believed that all the allied nations should contribute to the common pool for the common cause. But when we are discussing additional loans- I say this to the Minister of Finance particularly-to nations it seems to me that the situation is entirely different. In such cases I have no hesitation in urging the freeing of Canada from any of her external debts by the repatriation of securities held abroad.
To-day I want to make some comments in connection with the costs of certain goods which go to make up the gift that we are
Mutual Aid Bill

making to the allied nations. As I have said already, we support the free transfer of war goods to our allies, but we criticize severely profits and gifts to private corporations which these transfers involve. Under the necessities of war, giant monopolies in Canada are strengthening their economic control and endangering the future of democracy in the country in which wm live. Of these monopolies I think the outstanding example at the moment is the Aluminum Company of Canada. Since I mentioned this company and its operations in March, certain other information has come to my knowledge which I intend to place before the house and the government, because I believe that this information bears directly on the matter of supplying necessary commodities to the united nations.
First let me say that I understand that some eighty per cent of the stock of the Aluminum Company of Canada is owned by the people who control the stock of the Aluminum Company of the United States. The Canadian company obviously was organized originally as a separate corporation to escape the United States anti-trust laws in order that this company might be able to play its part in the international cartel whose agreements restricted production in t'he democratic countries and allowed Germany greatly to expand her aluminum production before the war. The history of these companies is a story of the manner in which monopoly obtains privileges and makes profits.
In the fifty years from its original incorporation in 1888 the parent company has made profits of over $335,000,000. In the first twenty-four years, from 1888 to 1912, it made profits of $33,000,000. This on an original investment of $2,000,000. The net profit in 1940 was $44,000,000. In 1941 the Canadian company had net profits of $13,992,000 after paying income taxes and excess profits taxes.
What invested capital earned that profit?
The invested capital was built up largely out of profits and reserves of the company.
But the sums were large.

The sums were large; nevertheless you cannot consider them apart from their origin. It is to this giant corporation that the governments concerned have given or advanced hundreds of millions of dollars to enable them to build a huge plant at Shipshaw and to expand their aluminum monopoly. How was this huge expansion financed? This is where we enter more directly into a discussion of the provisions of

the bill. Part of Canada's contribution, although not all, is covered by P.C. 11745, which provides for a special write-off or accelerated depreciation of $154,500,000. The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) gave a break-down of this to the house in March. I have the prospectus of the company, and it has the following to say about Canada's contribution:
Normally, such capital expenditures for plant additions are written off for tax purposes over a period of years. In order to give effect to the fundamental basis of the contracts, permission has been granted the company to amortize these capital expenditures by a special deduction from income at a stipulated rate per pound of all aluminum delivered-
I understand that is five and a half cents per pound.
-the effect being to amortize the estimated cost of the additional aluminum producing facilities and sixty per cent of the estimated cost of the additional power facilities by the time all deliveries have been made under the war contracts.
Would the hon. member identify that prospectus?

This is the prospectus dealing with the new 1942 issue of $15,000,000 five per cent preferred stock by the Aluminum Company of Canada. Thus all the aluminum facilities will be retired by a special write-off from income, and sixty per cent of the cost of the power plant will be retired under the war contracts of the company. In addition to this $154,500,000 there are various pieces of equipment and some projects at Kingston and Arvida which are depreciated in one or two years. The amount of these depreciations is some $9,000,000. There is also provision for another amount of $9,000,000 for the protection of the company against abnormal costs. According to sessional paper 274 tabled in the house there appear to be eighteen other projects of the company totalling $4,431,000, nine of which, totalling $3,869,000, are to be written off in a year, and the other nine, totalling $562,000, in two years. It seems to me therefore that the total is not $154,500,000, as we were told in the house this year, but nearer to $175,000,000.
The necessities of war and the monopolistic position in which this company found itself has enabled it to take from the nations in their war extremity hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of property in addition to the profits they are able to make in the meantime. The British contribution is referred to on page 5 of the prospectus as follows:
The total loan was increased to $55,600,000, which figure appears in the consolidated balance

Mutual Aid Bill
sheet printed herewith as "3 per cent redeemable notes, due 1961, payable to the British government-principal and interest abatable in certain circumstances as provided in the contracts under which they were issued." These loans are payable in full if all of the additional capacity is used in each of the twenty years during the life of the notes. If in any year or years such additional capacity is used only in part, the notes are payable only in proportionate part, both as to principal and interest.
It should be noted that the British loan is repayable in full only if all the additional capacity is used in each of the twenty years during the life of the notes.

Just to clarify that, the additional capacity referred to is capacity additional to the first capacity built. If there is any future to the aluminum business these notes are likely to be paid in full.

The minister said on
March 23 that the outlook after the war was more or less problematical.

The outlook to which my
hon. friend referred is not the outlook of that part of the plant that is covered by the loan.

I am glad to get the
minister's statement, but if none of the additional capacity is used in any year, then that year's repayment is cancelled. I think that is true. Let us remember that the British government was paying two cents a pound more for its aluminum than the United States government pays for lease-lend aluminum.

No, both prices were adjusted
on the same date. The price in the United States at the time the British were paying seventeen cents per pound was exactly the same price converted into United States dollars. When the price was cut to fifteen cents the Canadian price was revised accordingly to all customers. There was some discussion between the officers of the Aluminum company and the officers of the Reconstruction Finance corporation or the Metals corporation with regard to maintaining the differential, but naturally the Canadian government had something to-say about that. The change that was made in price was made simultaneously for all customers.

I am very glad to
know that. But my information-I will tell the minister what my information was-was that all the aluminum used by the United States for other than lease-lend purposes was still chargeable at fifteen cents and the aluminum used for lease-lend purposes was chargeable at seventeen cents and that the British were also paying seventeen cents.
No, that was the first proposal. It was referred to in congress but it is not true. When the final agreement was made that was adjusted.

I am very glad to get
that correction, and as I proceed if there are any other misstatements of fact I hope the minister will correct me.
Looking over the prospectus I am forced to the conclusion that the British parliament ought to investigate the circumstances under which the agreement was made and who made it on their behalf. I am not going to discuss that because, as I say, it is a matter for the British parliament to deal with. There has been a good deal of talk about the American contribution. Let us see what the prospectus says. The prospectus says:
From an original total of approximately $93,000,000, they have now been reduced as a result of metal deliveries to approximately $79,000,000. As new smelters come into operation, the liquidation of these advance payments is being accelerated. Cancellation of future deliveries under such contracts by the purchasers prior to the completion thereof (the greater part of which are to be made before the end of 1944) would relieve the company of the obligation to repay practically all of the balance of the advance payments not then liquidated.
No doubt the part played by these advance payments by the United States will be thoroughly investigated at Washington. It is not my purpose to criticize the activities of any government of a friendly or allied nation. I take it that that is a matter for their own people and for their own congress.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply argued that the American participation in the plant had reduced the price from seventeen to fifteen cents per pound.
No, I did not argue that.
The minister mentioned that in the course of his remarks on March 23.
No. The North American price dropped.

I am glad the minister has cleared up that point because there is in the prospectus something which lends colour to the idea that there are two different prices. I will refer the minister to the words used in the prospectus, as follows:
Despite making provision for the payment of the major part of the cost of w-ar facilities from the proceeds of the metal sold, the company has reduced the base selling price of aluminum approximately twenty per cent since the outbreak of the war.
That gave some colour to the idea that there were two different prices-a base price and another. I am glad to know, therefore, that that new price applies to all the united nations.

The Prime Minister has announced that he is going to Washington. I think it would be well for him while there to inquire into all the matters concerning the signing of Canada's agreement; for I want to ask him what part in this agreement and in the general agreement we are discussing the Department of External Affaire played. What part did it play in relation to this country? I note that the report of the Canadian Legation at AVashing-ton for the year 1942 refers to the many and complicated questions, including taxation, dealt with by the legation. This depreciation, of course, is very largely a matter of discussion with our taxing authorities.

I think I can answer that now. The legation played absolutely no part in the discussion. The Department of Munitions and Supply was familiar with certain phases, but the transaction was carried out directly between the Aluminum Company of Canada and the Metals Reserve bank.
Did the Department of Munitions and Supply make arrangements regarding accelerated depreciation?
No.
Well, who did?
They were recommended to the cabinet by the war contracts depreciation board.

I am not disputing the minister's word. I am just questioning his knowledge. I find it very difficult to believe that the minister at Washington had nothing to do with negotiations in regard to these matters involving Canada and the United States. I am saying this because I think it is something of which this house, and particularly the Prime Minister, should take heed now. Our minister at Washington is Mr. Leighton McCarthy. I understand that while it is obligatory for ministers of the crown to resign their directorates in companies, it is also customary but not obligatory for ministers to foreign countries to resign their directorates also. Mr. McCarthy, right up to January of this year, was a director of the Aluminum Company of Canada. He is still a director and vice-president of the parent company, the Aluminum Company of the United States. Had he remained a director of the Aluminum Company of Canada he would probably have signed this prospectus to which I have made frequent reference this afternoon, but he resigned shortly before it was issued and after the deal was made. As a matter of fact, Mr. McCarthy has been for thirty years legal consultant to the Aluminum Company of
[Mr. Coldwell.J
Canada, and the prospectus is signed by J. F. Van Lane, as a director. Mr. Van Lane is the secretary of McCarthy and McCarthy of Toronto, the minister's old legal firm.

Mr. Speaker, may I say that for my hon. friend to attack a man in Mr. McCarthy's position is most unwarranted. Mr. McCarthy is a man who had retired from active business, a man who had reached an age when he might well have been permitted to retire, but as a patriotic duty he accepted, under considerable pressure, the post he now occupies at Washington. I have assured my hon. friend that I know from my own personal knowledge that Mr. McCarthy had absolutely no contact with this transaction. Why attempt to injure a man in Mr. McCarthy's position, a man who cannot defend himself on this floor, particularly when I have stated the true facts?

Mr. Speaker, I am not injuring Mr. McCarthy, but I am going to place before this house a condition which I think is against the best interests of this country. Mr. McCarthy may have done nothing improper, but I say that a government in appointing gentlemen to represent this country abroad should insist upon their relinquishing their association with business, particularly business of this description which may be involved in negotiations between our two countries. Mr. McCarthy is a director of a number of power companies which, like the aluminum company group, have used every means possible to prevent the development of public power in this country, particularly St. Lawrence power. In my opinion this whole deal demands a thorough investigation, and the Prime Minister when he is in Washington should see Mr. McCarthy and discuss his own position with him. Personally I think that Mr. McCarthy should be asked to come back to Canada and explain to the government why it is that he has retained these directorates in spite of custom. The Aluminum Company of Canada is associated with the Saguenay power and other power enterprises in Canada. Often our two countries are discussing electric power relationships, and this house should know that the New York state power authorities, the government organization, in its annual report for 1937 named Mr. McCarthy as one of the men blocking the development of the St. Lawrence waterways as a public enterprise. The New York power authority also named Canada Life Assurance, of which Mr. McCarthy and Arthur W. Davis, brother of the president of Aluminum of America, after whom

Mutual Aid Bill
Arvida is called, who are directors, as associated with numerous power companies in blocking public power enterprises. The New York report says:
The people of New York and Ontario face the necessity of overcoming the influence of this consortium of monopoly interests if they are to realize the wealth producing capabilities of their chief waterpower resources in the St. Lawrence and Niagara rivers.
This whole aluminum deal is linked very closely with power and power interests. It is not only aluminum they want. It is the great power resource, Shipshaw, the greatest in Canada, yes, the greatest developed in the world, which these people are anxious to control and are controlling. There is one thing about this prospectus which struck me at once. This is an invitation to subscribe $15,000,000 par value of five per cent cumulative redeemable sinking fund preferred shares. Why the preference shares now for the first time in the company's history. It has authority to issue three million shares of common stock. They have only issued $1,500,000 of common shares, and I am advised by people who have made inquiries that if one wants to get preferred shares the limit is twenty-five shares. Why? Because they want to give the small investor a chance to get in first, they say. In my opinion, what they really wish to do is to spread some of the preferred shares over the country in order that there will be public opinion favourable to the aluminum company. That is the trick of utility corporations everywhere; and as for this common stock held in the treasury, if this venture is what we think it may be, anything may be done with it, and the people who control the company may obtain a great deal of unearned increment out of it.
On March 23 the Minister of Munitions and Supply said that in the dim and distant future the aluminum company may obtain some benefit from the Shipshaw development and there may be some post-war value in it for them. I say that these power aluminum interests have obtained in effect the greatest power resources at present available in the world, virtually as a gift; and thus they can, if they will, effectively block, in Ontario and New York state and eastern North America as well, any government-owned public power development, because their plant will be paid for during the war and any plant which the province of Ontario or the government of New York state, or the government of Canada or that of the United States or both, may wish to build, will have to be paid for over a period of years. Not only that, but they
will be able, through the cheapness of power, to control the price of aluminum almost everywhere on earth, and when we realize that we are entering upon an age of light metals and that they have entered into the field of magnesium production as well, we can understand how dangerous a monopoly we are building up by our public funds and war activities in this country.
Indeed, I believe that the real objective is the control of these great power resources by this corporation. Those of us who have lived long enough in Canada to know about the struggle that has gone on over a period of years between, on the one hand, Insul-until he was eliminated by the depression-and the great North American power trust, and on the other hand the publicly-owned enterprises, will realize the force of what I am saying. I believe that is behind all this, and in making this great gift, into every pound of munitions that we give, containing aluminum, five and a half cents a pound is a charge, aiding this company further to establish its monopoly control of these great power and metal resources.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that under these circumstances the government would be warranted, this house would be warranted, in appointing a royal commission to go into all the phases of this deal and to see what the implications are to the public of Canada and of the United States.
I am not going to continue at greater length. I have tried to condense in as few words as possible what I had to say this afternoon but I feel that this house cannot overlook what is going on in Canada. In common with many other people, I am gravely disturbed and alarmed over the trend of events in Canada. Some people say that we are opposed to free enterprise. I am not opposed to free enterprise. I should like to see every man free to follow his abilities and his initiative. I am opposed, however, to what one of the representatives before the committee yesterday called corporate enterprise, and if we are to continue as we are going we shall be delivered completely into the hands of these corporations and we shall have, as someone behind me suggests, not a cooperative commonwealth but a corporate state. When we examine the various phases of the war appropriation measure we shall go into a number of related matters. The policy is wrong. It is anti-social, it is unsound from the point of view of the people; and in passing this bill I urge that we do so with our eyes open. We wish to make the gift, but in making the gift I fear the government unfortunately is fastening on our people giant corporations like the one I have discussed this afternoon. .
